title: array, vector, and span: ownership and views
lead: Choose a container according to size requirements and pass its data to a function without losing bounds.
why: A pointer alone does not carry a length, and manual allocation distracts from the algorithm. Standard containers provide an explicit size and lifetime foundation.
objectives: Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not use a span after vector reallocation; create it after filling the vector.
prerequisites: Modules 1–2: expressions, comparisons, types, references, and checked cin.
Follow the prerequisite links: cpp.functions-contracts. New constructs are introduced before the assignment.

concepts.definition: an object managing the lifetime of stored elements.
access to another object’s elements under an explicit lifetime constraint.
vector storage capacity before reallocation is needed.
increasing available capacity without creating elements.
loss of validity of an earlier address or view.

sections.title: Why three types exist
paragraphs: std::array<int,3> is an object containing three ints with its size encoded in the type. std::vector<int> owns a sequence whose size can change. std::span<const int> is a non-owning view of existing ints and their count.

Angle brackets supply arguments to a library template: the element type and, for array, the extent. You do not need to author a template yet. Include <array>, <vector>, and <span> for their corresponding names.

sections.title: Size is not capacity
paragraphs: vector.size() counts existing elements; capacity() counts how many can fit without reallocation. reserve(10) provides capacity but leaves size at zero. After reserve, v[0] is invalid until push_back or resize has created that element.

push_back(value) appends an element; empty() tests size()==0. Teaching programs bound the sequence to at most 100 values. In an exception-disabled environment, allocation failure is not promised to be catchable; do not use it as normal input validation.

sections.title: Traversal and auto
paragraphs: for(int value : values) obtains a copy of each element. for(const auto& value : values) reads without copying; auto deduces a static type and is not dynamic typing. Mutating elements requires a non-const auto& reference.

Use an index when position matters. Compare it with size() and avoid subtracting one from a zero unsigned size. Prove !empty() before accessing the last element; front and back also require a nonempty container.

sections.title: span passes a range
paragraphs: sum(std::span<const int> values) accepts a read-only range. Compatible arrays, vectors, and built-in arrays can supply it. Inside, size(), empty(), [], and range-for are available; the function does not own the elements’ memory.

An empty span is valid when the algorithm handles it. In C++20 these types’ operator[] is not input validation: the index must be below size(). Do not execute out-of-bounds accesses as demonstrations; identify the violated precondition on paper.

sections.title: View lifetime
paragraphs: The owner must remain alive throughout span use. When a growing vector reallocates, pointers, references, and spans into the old buffer become invalid. reserve may reduce reallocations but cannot replace a lifetime argument.

Finish modifying a container before creating a short-lived span, then process it without resizing the owner. Do not retain a view into a local vector after its function returns. const in span<const int> restricts writes through the view but does not extend lifetime.

sections.title: Choice and evidence
paragraphs: Use array for a small fixed set, vector for a dynamic count, and span for a viewing parameter. This separates storage from the algorithm. Linear summation needs O(n) time and O(1) additional memory regardless of the owner.

Test the same function with three owners and an empty view. Separately record size before and after reserve and push_back. Next, compare these abstractions with a traditional array while preserving identical boundary rules.

assessment.question: What does reserve(10) change for an empty vector?
answers: Capacity, but not the element count

assessment.question: Who owns span data?
assessment.explanation: A view does not extend its owner lifetime.

assessment.question: When is v[0] valid?
assessment.explanation: Capacity does not imply an element exists.

assessment.question: What may happen to a span after vector reallocation?
assessment.explanation: Create the view after resizing the owner.
